common_name: Professor Anton Kippenberg Aster (Compact Semi-Double Lavender-Blue New York Aster)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Professor Anton Kippenberg is a compact New York Aster with semi-double lavender-blue flowers, holder of the RHS Award of Garden Merit.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; unlike many drought-tolerant native asters, New York Aster cultivars perform best with consistent moisture. Professor Anton Kippenberg is a compact, long-cultivated selection bearing masses of semi-double, lavender-blue, yellow-centered daisies in early to mid fall, its dwarf habit and reliable form having earned it the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit over many decades of garden use. Divide clumps every two to three years in spring to maintain vigor and reduce the powdery mildew that can affect crowded New York Aster plantings, and pinch stems back by a third in early summer for a bushier, more floriferous plant.

common_name: Little Carlow Aster (Vigorous Hybrid Lavender-Blue Autumn Aster)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Little Carlow is a vigorous hybrid aster bearing masses of small lavender-blue, yellow-centered daisies in autumn, holder of the RHS Award of Garden Merit.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light partial shade. Little Carlow, a vigorous hybrid believed to derive from Aster cordifolius parentage, produces an exceptionally heavy late-season display of small, lavender-blue, yellow-centered daisies held in airy, branching sprays above heart-shaped lower leaves, earning it the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit. It tolerates light shade better than most asters and shows good resistance to powdery mildew. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring, and stake or grow among sturdy neighbors if grown in rich soil, since strong growth can flop under the weight of bloom.

common_name: Harrington's Pink Aster (Heirloom Tall Salmon-Pink New England Aster)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Harrington's Pink is a tall heirloom New England Aster selection with soft salmon-pink single flowers, introduced in the 1930s.

directions: Plant in moist, average to fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Harrington's Pink is a long-cultivated heirloom selection of the native New England Aster, introduced in the 1930s and still valued for its soft, clear salmon-pink single flowers, a distinctive warm tone among the mostly purple- and violet-flowered native asters, blooming heavily on tall stems in early to mid fall. It is a valuable late-season nectar source for migrating monarch butterflies and other pollinators. Pinch stems back by a third in early summer to encourage a bushier, less floppy habit, and divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring.

common_name: Prairie Aster (Smooth Glaucous-Stemmed Native Violet-Blue Aster)

planting.note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification, or plant divisions in spring, in well-drained soil in full sun; Prairie Aster is a smooth, glaucous-stemmed native species with violet-blue flowers on airy, branching panicles.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; established plants tolerate considerable drought thanks to a deep taproot. Prairie Aster is a native prairie and glade species with smooth, pale, glaucous stems and narrow leaves, bearing airy, widely branching panicles of violet-blue, yellow-centered flowers in fall, a graceful, open form well suited to native and pollinator gardens across the central and southern plains. It provides late-season nectar for bees and butterflies. Cut back in late winter before new growth emerges, and divide congested clumps every few years in spring if desired, though the plant spreads modestly and rarely needs it.

common_name: White Panicle Aster (Native Rhizomatous White-Flowered Aster)

planting.note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification, or plant divisions in spring, in moist to average soil in full sun to light partial shade; White Panicle Aster is a native rhizomatous species bearing abundant small white flowers in branched panicles.

directions: Plant in moist to average, well-drained soil in full sun to light partial shade; this adaptable native tolerates both wet meadow conditions and drier average garden soil. White Panicle Aster spreads by rhizomes to form colonies, bearing an abundance of small, white, yellow-centered flowers in loosely branched panicles from late summer into fall, valuable as a late-season nectar source for bees, butterflies, and migrating monarchs. Because it spreads readily, site it where it can naturalize in a native planting, meadow, or rain garden rather than a tightly controlled formal border, or divide and thin clumps every year or two to keep it in bounds.
